worked_example.title: Read the denominators before the percentage

blocks.title: Same overall score different class results
blocks.caption: Overall accuracy weights classes by their number of evaluation examples. Balanced accuracy gives the two class-specific fractions equal weight.

blocks.label: Both methods score 80 percent. Explain which cases the baseline fails, how the candidate changes the errors, and why their balanced accuracies differ.

blocks.text: Balanced accuracy is a metric choice, not a repair to the classifier or a guarantee of safety. It gives classes equal influence in this summary; it does not encode the actual consequences of false alarms and missed cases. Four blocked evaluation examples are also too few for a strong general claim.

guided_practice.title: Compare both class fractions
guided_practice.prompt: For the worked candidate [[12,4],[0,4]], give ordinary accuracy, both class-specific correct fractions, balanced accuracy, false positives and false negatives. Compare with the baseline.
guided_practice.answer: Accuracy 16/20=80 percent. Clear fraction 12/16=75 percent; blocked fraction 4/4=100 percent; balanced accuracy (75+100)/2=87.5 percent. FP=4,FN=0. Baseline accuracy is also 80 percent but balanced accuracy is 50 percent with FP=0,FN=4.

independent_case.title: Assess a new comparison independently
independent_case.task: New training labels have a clear majority. A separate evaluation has 18 clear and 2 blocked records. The always-clear baseline is [[18,0],[2,0]] and candidate is [[15,3],[1,1]], with reference rows and clear then blocked on both axes. Calculate ordinary accuracy, both class fractions and balanced accuracy for each. Give candidate FP and FN, then explain why the metrics do not choose an automatic winner.
independent_case.answer: Baseline accuracy 18/20=90 percent; class fractions 100 percent and 0 percent; balanced accuracy 50 percent. Candidate accuracy 16/20=80 percent; clear fraction 15/18=5/6 about 83.3 percent, blocked fraction 1/2=50 percent; balanced accuracy (5/6+1/2)/2=2/3 about 66.7 percent. Candidate FP=3,FN=1. It finds one blocked case but adds three false alarms; task consequences and the small sample matter.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

misconceptions: High accuracy means both classes work well
A common class can dominate the overall count. Inspect each reference-class denominator and its errors.
It changes the summary weighting, not any prediction or underlying error.
An absent class has zero measured performance
Its fraction has a zero denominator and is unavailable. Report missing coverage rather than inventing a value.

blocks.text: A closer explanation

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
def scores(counts):
    clear_n = sum(counts[0])
    blocked_n = sum(counts[1])
    if clear_n == 0 or blocked_n == 0:
        raise ValueError("Need evaluation examples of both classes")
    correct = counts[0][0] + counts[1][1]
    accuracy = correct / (clear_n + blocked_n)
    clear_fraction = counts[0][0] / clear_n
    blocked_fraction = counts[1][1] / blocked_n
    balanced = (clear_fraction + blocked_fraction) / 2
    return accuracy, balanced

baseline = [[16, 0], [4, 0]]
candidate = [[12, 4], [0, 4]]
for name, counts in [("baseline", baseline), ("candidate", candidate)]:
    accuracy, balanced = scores(counts)
    print(name, round(100 * accuracy, 1), round(100 * balanced, 1))

The output is baseline 80.0 50.0, then candidate 80.0 87.5. In each output line the first percentage is ordinary accuracy and the second is balanced accuracy. For the candidate, the clear-class correct fraction is 12/16=75 percent and the blocked-class fraction is 4/4=100 percent. Their equal average is 87.5 percent.

For the baseline, those fractions are 16/16=100 percent and 0/4=0 percent, averaging 50 percent. The code assumes a two-by-two table of nonnegative integer counts in the stated order. It stops when either reference class is absent. Then report the observed counts and the unavailable class result; do not invent a denominator or silently substitute zero.

blocks.text: The printed proportion is 0.75, or 75 percent, among four known responses. Yes among all five supplied responses is 0.6, or 60 percent. Both calculations are correct when labelled; they describe different denominators. Unknown must not silently become No.
Name the group behind a percentage

Count the responses before dividing. In the example, three say Yes, one says No and one is Unknown. There are four known responses, so Yes among known responses is 3 divided by 4, or 75 percent. Yes among all five supplied responses is 3 divided by 5, or 60 percent. Neither number needs to be hidden. Label the question each answers, and keep the unknown count visible.
